title: Where Trust Ends Is Where Consent Begins

questions.question: Which two components sit inside the user's trust domain in an MCP system?
options: The host and its client, since the user installed and connected them
The server and its tool, which run inside the user's own account
Only the model itself, since it is the one part users never installed
The transport layer alone, since it moves messages between every part
questions.explanation: The host embeds the client the user's application controls directly, while the server is a separate program the user did not write, so trust follows who controls the code, not where the connection happens to run.

questions.question: A client calls a tool tagged as side-effecting. What must be true before the server should let the call proceed?
options: The tool's description must read as a polite request, not a command
The user must have already given explicit consent scoped to that tool
The client must keep retrying the call until the server accepts it
The host must first upgrade the connection to a newer protocol version
questions.explanation: A side-effecting call changes something outside the conversation, so a conformant design requires the user's explicit approval for that specific tool before the server runs it, rather than treating politeness, retries, or transport speed as a substitute for consent.

questions.question: Why is a tool result treated as untrusted content when it reaches the model?
options: Because JSON-RPC replies are always sent without transport encryption
Because the model cannot parse any structured data an external call returns
Because it comes from a separate, unverified program outside the host
Because every server intentionally corrupts the data it sends to a client
questions.explanation: The server is code the host did not write and cannot fully verify, so whatever text or data a tool call returns is treated as input from an outside source, the same caution applied to any content a model reads from beyond its own application.

questions.question: A host has consent recorded for a tool named send_email. A different tool named send_sms is now called. What should happen?
options: The call proceeds because both tools share the same word send in their name
The call proceeds because consent for any messaging tool covers all messaging tools
The call proceeds because the earlier consent grant applies for the rest of the session
The call is refused because consent was scoped to send_email and not to send_sms
questions.explanation: Consent attaches to one named tool, not to a category implied by a shared word in its name or a session-wide grant, so a different tool must clear the same gate on its own regardless of how similar its purpose looks.

questions.question: A design auto-approves every tool call, read-only or side-effecting, the first time a server connects. What risk does this introduce?
options: No risk, since the handshake already authenticates the server's identity
One blanket approval skips consent for every side-effecting call it makes
The server becomes completely unable to advertise any tool that it exposes
The client can no longer send any read-only call for the rest of that session
questions.explanation: Approving a server once instead of gating each side-effecting call collapses the distinction the protocol relies on, so an action that changes something outside the conversation runs with the same lack of friction as a call that only reads data.

questions.question: A read-only tool like list_files is called without any prior consent grant. Under the model this lesson teaches, what happens?
options: The call is refused, since every tool call needs consent regardless of effect
The call is queued until the user manually approves the read-only tool
The call proceeds, since it carries no side effect that requires any approval
The call fails, since the server cannot tell read-only tools from others
questions.explanation: A call that only reads data does not change anything outside the conversation, so the design lets it proceed without a consent prompt, while still keeping the option to require consent for reads in a context where even reading counts as sensitive.
